A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the connectivity among NTMR networks is more important than the size and number of NTMRs.

we were able to infer larval dispersal distances and connectivity patterns for a reef-fish species in the Philippines, and that these patterns validated the design of the NTMR network that was established there in the early 2000s.
the genetic data from this study provide strong evidence that NTMR networks can be effective for sustaining coral-reef fishes, even in areas where larval connectivity is relatively low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NTMR networks are not a panacea for reef-fish management, as the success of NTMR networks depends critically on the strength of larval connectivity among NTMR populations.
NTMR networks can be effective in sustaining reef-fish populations, but only if the networks are managed collaboratively across political or customary jurisdictions.
the design of NTMR networks should be based on the dispersal characteristics of the focal taxa, and the design of NTMRS should be based on their connectivity to other NTMRs and fished areas.
